entries.title: JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28
entries.summary: JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving heap memory preparation onto concurrent worker threads. ZGC now pre-touches memory as it expands and upgrades small pages to large ones on Linux 6.1 and later, but the 2 MB initial heap behind the JEP's 38% startup and 90% warmup gains requires the adaptive heap sizing flag from JEP 546, which is off by default. B
entries.content:
JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving the work of acquiring and preparing heap memory off the startup path and onto dedicated concurrent worker threads. On Linux 6.1 and later it also upgrades 4 KB pages to 2 MB pages while the application runs. The 2 MB initial heap behind the JEP's headline numbers comes from elsewhere: adaptive heap sizing, in the companion JEP 546, which still defaults to off.

Deploying ZGC has until now meant choosing which half of a trade-off to pay for. The collector's pause times do not grow with the heap, but its collection frequency does, so a small heap brings on early and frequent cycles. The JEP describes the older ergonomic behavior of committing one sixty-fourth of physical memory for the initial heap.

A team chasing fast startup set a tiny 

-Xms
and accepted a long warmup, because the collector then had to acquire and prepare memory in increments while the application was already allocating. A team chasing fast warmup set a large 
-Xms
, usually with 
-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
, and paid the whole bill before the first request landed. The JEP puts the spread at roughly a tenth of a second to start with a 2 MB heap against more than ten seconds with a 32 GB one on current hardware.

That work now happens in a new thread, 

ZMemoryWorker
, one per heap partition. It commits and uncommits memory concurrently as capacity changes. It also heats memory before application threads reach it, which means pre-touching page by page and collapsing small pages into large ones.

The budget is fixed rather than adaptive. 

ZConcurrentWorkersCPUShare
in 
zGlobals.hpp
is 0.25, so preparation takes at most a quarter of the available CPU. ZGC's director caps young-generation worker counts when adaptive sizing is on, which keeps collection inside its CPU target while expansion continues and the collector deliberately runs above its heuristic heap size target.

Large pages on Linux no longer require an administrator to reserve them up front. ZGC probes for 

MADV_COLLAPSE
, the 
madvise
mode added in Linux 6.1, by mapping a 4 MB region, pre-touching a single page and collapsing an aligned 2 MB range. When the probe succeeds and memory heating is enabled, the collector enters a new 
Collapse
state and upgrades pages in the background. The call races the kernel's 
khugepaged
, so the implementation retries on 
EAGAIN
.

The change shows up in what a deployer no longer has to decide. Where JDK 25 forced a choice between two tunings, JDK 28 offers a third option:

JDK 25, tuned for startup

$ java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms2m -Xmx32g -jar app.jar

JDK 25, tuned for warmup

$ java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms32g -Xmx32g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch -jar app.jar

JDK 28, neither trade-off

$ java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZAdaptiveHeapSizing -jar app.jar

The third command produces the JEP's case study figures, a 38% drop in startup time and a fall in warmup from 80 seconds to 10 for Spring PetClinic on a 32 GB machine. 

-XX:+ZAdaptiveHeapSizing
takes the minimum and initial heap down to 2 MB and raises the 
MaxHeapSize
ceiling to 100% of physical memory. Without it, ZGC falls back to the shared heap sizing path and a 25% ceiling. Concurrent preparation still runs, but not the aggressive expansion the measurements depend on.

Using identical memory techniques on every operating system is an explicit non-goal, so large pages may be the default on Linux and not on Windows. The JEP also cautions that applications tuned around a larger initial heap may warm up more slowly and need re-tuning.

Two further edges live in the implementation rather than the text. Pairing 

-XX:+UseLargePages
with adaptive sizing and no 
-Xmx
logs a warning and disables explicit large pages for the heap. The retry loop around 
MADV_COLLAPSE
can also spin indefinitely when 
EAGAIN
persists, a case the code attributes to pinning through 
mlock
or long-term DMA and treats as user error.

Teams can see the heap sizing difference for themselves on the JDK 28 early-access builds by comparing the resolved flags:

$ java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "MinHeapSize|InitialHeapSize|MaxHeapSize"
$ java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZAdaptiveHeapSizing -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "MinHeapSize|InitialHeapSize|MaxHeapSize"

The second run drops the minimum and initial sizes to the 2 MB floor and lifts the maximum from a quarter of physical memory to all of it. Adding 

-Xlog:gc+init
reports 
Memory Heating: Enabled
and, once the collapse path is active, 
Large Page Support: Enabled (Transparent, JVM enforced)
.

Services already running a modest heap on Linux 6.1 or later pick up concurrent pre-touch and background large pages without touching a flag, because memory heating is on by default. Services carrying a large pre-touched heap purely to buy warmup have something to delete, though only after enabling adaptive sizing. That 100% ceiling reads worse than it behaves. The policy tracks machine-wide memory and holds a reserve, preferring to leave a fifth of the machine free, fighting for a tenth and enforcing a twentieth, with those margins widening when usage is unstable or compressed.

JDK 28 reaches Rampdown Phase One on December 3, 2026, with general availability scheduled for March 9, 2027. The JEP's own future work points at better CPU sharing between concurrent collection and concurrent commit, and at ahead-of-time compilation from JEP 544, already Completed for JDK 28, which frees JIT cycles the memory workers could spend instead.

entries.title: Java News Roundup: Java4Shell, Oracle CSPUs, OpenJDK, Azul Payara, BellSoft, Helidon, LangChain4j
entries.summary: This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive. By Michael Redlich
entries.content:
This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive.

OpenJDK

Oracle has released versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3, 11.0.33.0.3 and 8u511b3 of the JDK as part of their quarterly Critical Security Patch Update Advisory for November 2026. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes for version 27.0.1.0.3, version 25.0.5.0.3, version 21.0.13.0.3, version 17.0.21.0.3, version 11.0.33.0.3 and version 8u511 b33.

JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Proposed to Target to Targeted for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of 

final
fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case.

JEP 548, Vector API (Thirteenth Incubator), has been elevated from its JEP Draft 8397768 to Candidate status. This JEP proposes a thirteenth incubation with one notable change, after twelve rounds of incubation delivered in JDK 16 through JDK 27. This feature introduces an API to "express vector computations that reliably compile at runtime to optimal vector instructions on supported CPU architectures, thus achieving performance superior to equivalent scalar computations." This JEP adds support for 

 vectors, whose lanes hold 16-bit floating-point numbers in the IEEE 754 Vector
binary16
 format. The Vector API will continue to incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features. At that time, the Vector API team will adapt the Vector API and its implementation to use them, and will promote the Vector API from Incubation to Preview.
    
JDK 28

    
Build 25 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 24 that include fixes for various issues. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

    
For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

    
Java4Shell

    
A new Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability, known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), affects versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3 and 8u511b33-perf of Oracle Java SE, versions 21.0.13.0.3 and 17.0.21.0.3 of Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. As described in the CVE documentation:

    


[This] difficult to exploit vulnerability allows [an] unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Note: This vulnerability can only be exploited by supplying data to APIs in the specified Component without using Untrusted Java Web Start applications or Untrusted Java applets, such as through a web service.

    
Organizations and projects that have addressed this CVE include: BellSoft, Azul, JetBrains, GraalVM, Quarkus and WildFly. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

    
Spring Framework

    
It was a busy week over at Spring as the various teams have delivered GA releases that include: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Security, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOAS, Spring Modulith, Spring AI, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka and Spring LDAP.

    
The Spring team has also resolved a total of 90 CVEs spanning multiple projects. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

    
Azul Payara

    
The release of Azul Payara 7.6.0, the November 2026 edition, includes Community Edition 7.2026.11, Enterprise Edition 6.44.0 and Enterprise Edition 5.93.0. Along with bug fixes and component upgrades, all three editions deliver resolutions to five CVEs, two of which are related to Azul Payara:

    
    
      
  • CVE-2026-90908, a vulnerability in the 
    GenericAdminAuthenticator
     class that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to bypass JMX/RMI administrative access restrictions by spoofing the client host address that may lead to remote code execution.
    • 
      
  • CVE-2026-110003, A vulnerability in the administration REST interface that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to bypass secure-admin remote-access restrictions by supplying an arbitrary value in the 
    X-GlassFish-authToken
     HTTP header that grants execution of arbitrary administrative commands, equivalent to complete compromise of the server.
    • 
    

    
Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and the Azul Payara security advisories page.

    
Hibernate

    
The second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0 ship with one single bug fix from the first release candidates, in which use of the Jakarta Persistence 
 annotation could cause a deadlock when a session holding the lock on the row of the generator table needed a new block of IDs.@TableGenerator
    
Version 5.0.0.CR2 will be the last release candidate. With the GA release of version 5.0.0.Final, it will be declared as end-of-life and focus will be on version 5.1.0.

    
More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR2 and version 5.0.0.CR2.

    
Java Operator SDK

    
The release of Java Operator SDK 5.7.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: the ability to enable virtual threads via construction in the 
 class or the Operator
josdk.use-virtual-threads
 property; and a new 
keepAlive()
 method, defined in the 
Operator
 class that starts a non-daemon thread to keep the JVM running until the operator is shut down. Version 5.7 is now built on Fabric8 Kubernetes Client 8.0. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
    
BellSoft

    
Concurrent with Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) for November 2026, BellSoft has released CSPU patches for versions 27.0.1.1 25.0.5.1, 21.0.13.1, 17.0.21.1, 11.0.33.1, 8u514 7u523 and 6u523 of Liberica JDK, their downstream distribution of OpenJDK, to address this list of CVEs. This release also includes a patch for the aforementioned Java4Shell Remote Code Execution vulnerability.

    
With an overall total of 111 fixes and backports, BellSoft states they have participated in eliminating 21 issues in all releases.

    
Helidon

    
The release of Helidon 27.0.2 delivers bug fixes and one notable change in which the default limit of decoded-input (strings, byte arrays, JSON, forms, and buffered multipart parts) for in-memory entity conversations has been increased to 1 mebibyte (MiB). More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

    
This release also aligns with the Oracle Critical Patch Updates for November 2026 and includes the Helidon 4.x and 3.x release trains as described in this blog post.

    
LangChain4j

    
The formal release (along with the thirty-fourth beta release) of LangChain4j 1.24.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: new 
 and DecisionSchedulerPlanner
 classes to serve as a decision model-based agentic pattern; and support for resuming suspended agentic systems in the DecisionModels
 class. Further details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the AgentMonitorrelease notes.
    
Micrometer

    
After two milestones and two releases candidates, the GA release of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: an optimization of the 
 and PrometheusMeterRegistry
 classes for collecting data snapshots; and a new MicrometerCollector
RowState
 inner class, defined in the 
 class, that eliminates the need to remove and re-register an instance of the existing MultiGauge
Row
 inner class. More details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.
    
Similarly, the GA release of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a simplification of baggage handles and lookups by directly storing the name of the handle and its metadata by eliminating use of the 
CompositeBaggage
 and Java 
 classes; and a refactor of the AtomicReference
 class for improved baggage propagation. Further details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the BaggageTextMapPropagatorrelease notes.

entries.title: Netflix at QConSF 2026: Retrofitting the SDLC for AI Coding Agents
entries.summary: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam of Netflix explained how the Commerce team retrofitted its SDLC so AI coding agents and engineers could ship together. The team wrote 45 architecture decision records for people and agents, added a review agent that posts only verified blockers, and serves per-domain GraphRAG context through a single MCP tool. By Andrew Hoblitzell
entries.content:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the company's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.

Khuzam argued that most of the work was not about agents at all, but about documentation, consistency and review.

Much of Commerce runs as server-driven UI, an approach Netflix has discussed at QCon before. A single screen-composition service behind the API gateway builds screens for iOS, Android, web and TV.

Khuzam opened with a mock company email announcing that every engineer now had Claude Code and asking how much faster everyone was shipping. The problem the team ran into next was summed up in one line.

Agents promised speed. But we spent 20 years building for humans.

The team's first attempt was having an agent migrate tests, and it took four tries. The team started with "migrate this file," then added instructions, then the APIs to use, then how to mock data.

The docs were also hard to find, since the agent's context window ran out before it found the right page. And they were inconsistent, because tests were not written the same way across the codebase.

Developers rated the internal framework at a Net Promoter Score of -3. Moving from one test to a whole feature, from screen to data to route to test, meant teaching the agent how the team builds.

Khuzam described the fix as context engineering, "getting what engineers know into what agents see." The team wrote 45 architecture decision records, each "written for people and for agents."

Each record covers the context, the decision, a pattern and an anti-pattern, and AI usage notes on what an agent should do. It also links to related docs and code, and the records now ship inside almost every repository.

To keep those records and more than 300 other documents findable, the team borrowed from how search engines read a site. An AGENTS.md file, the project instructions file that coding agents read before anything else, plays the part of robots.txt.

The second half of the talk followed code after an agent writes it. Khuzam noted that the CI pipeline is still deterministic, running builds, tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues and canaries.

What changed is how agents plug into each phase. A review agent pre-reviews each pull request against the docs and ADRs, flags anti-patterns and looks at what depends on the change.

Its first version left 23 comments on a single PR, starting with "Overall this PR looks great!" It now posts only verified blockers, each with evidence, a fix and the ADR rule it breaks. Engineers can add a revise label to have an agent read the review and push a fix to the same PR. Changes aren't yet auto-merged, and engineers own the code.

Khuzam reported no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service and 32% more pull requests year over year. Developer NPS rose from -3 to +25 over three quarters.

Ahead of the session, Khuzam framed the stakes on LinkedIn: "Agents can write code, but what gives us the confidence to ship Tier 0 services to 300M+ members without everything falling apart?"

Work that crosses services raised a harder question. A product engineer building one feature touches the payment API, billing, the gateway and every client, so the team had to decide who owns the context and how it follows the work.

Khuzam listed approaches that did not hold up. Loading every repository did not fit, Git submodules were brittle, a Git MCP server "sees one file, not the system," and shared copies went stale.

The team needed context that was accurate, portable across agents, owned per domain and kept fresh. It settled on GraphRAG per domain, taking structure from the code and meaning from the docs and ADRs.

Each graph is pinned to specific commits and served through a single Model Context Protocol tool. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, a Slack bot and CI review all query the same graph, and every answer cites a file and a line.

Khuzam closed with three rules: decide what agents should do and tell them, make it easy to find how to do it, and remember that human judgement still matters. "None of this is new. It's good engineering, built for a new reader."

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the session and can view the session details here.

entries.title: Agoda Reduces API Code Review Time by 64% with Modular Architecture
entries.summary: Agoda introduced a modular monolith framework in its post-booking API to reduce coupling without a full rewrite. The platform uses domain components, Data Mapper patterns, typed builders, and ArchUnit tests to enforce boundaries. Framework-backed changes showed 64% shorter median code reviews and 34% faster initial feedback than legacy changes. By Leela Kumili
entries.content:
Agoda has introduced a modular monolith framework in its post-booking API to reduce code coupling and enforce domain boundaries without rewriting the existing service. The approach combines component-based code organization, automated architecture checks, and incremental migration. The team reported 64% shorter median code review time and 34% shorter time to initial substantive feedback for framework-backed changes compared with legacy code.

The change addresses growing maintenance challenges in BAPI, which coordinates cancellations, booking amendments, refunds, and customer communications. Agoda extracted the API from its aging core monolith in 2019 through a largely line-by-line migration. As development increased, merge requests more than quadrupled between 2022 and 2025, while some files exceeded 4,000 lines.

The team characterized the migration as a tactical design trade-off, drawing on John K. Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design,

We had deliberately traded a strategic design approach for a tactical one to prioritize speed to market. This tactical mindset was exactly what the business needed at the time.

Rather than undertake a complete rewrite, the team introduced architectural boundaries incrementally.

The framework, called Platform, organizes code around business domains such as cancellations, rebooking, and payments rather than technical layers. Each component encapsulates its business logic and data access behind defined interfaces, with application, service, repository, and model layers contained within the component. This package-by-component approach aims to localize changes and reduce dependencies between business domains.

Platform framework boundaries inside a domain module (Source: Agoda Blog Post)

Agoda uses the Data Mapper pattern to keep repository-specific models, including database entities and API payloads, out of business logic. Typed builders centralize object creation and transformations, making it easier for developers to find where domain objects and service inputs are constructed.

The team also uses ArchUnit to encode architectural constraints as automated tests in continuous integration. For example, repository-specific models can only be accessed by their respective repositories. Violations fail the build rather than relying on code reviewers to identify unauthorized dependencies manually.

The team described these constraints as architectural fitness functions, a concept discussed by Neal Ford and Mark Richards in Software Architecture: The Hard Parts. One engineer explained:

By codifying our layer boundaries into an ArchUnit test suite, our CI pipeline serves as an automated guardrail, catching structural drift on every pull request before a human reviewer ever sees it.

Platform is now the default for new modules, while existing functionality is migrated incrementally when feature development provides an opportunity.

Agoda compared framework-backed and legacy merge requests in Q2 2026. Median review completion time was 1.08 hours for framework-backed changes, compared with 3.02 hours for legacy changes. Time to first substantive feedback was 10.34 hours versus 15.77 hours. Between June and August, framework-backed changes also used 29% fewer AI prompts per 100 changed lines, although median prompts per merge request were similar (20 vs. 22). Agoda cautioned that the AI findings were directional due to the short observation period. A related approach is Spring Modulith, which provides module verification and dependency-cycle checks for Spring Boot applications.

entries.title: Claude Code Adds Experimental Code Mode to Orchestrate Tool Calls with JavaScript
entries.summary: Anthropic's experimental Code Mode lets Claude Code write JavaScript that chains, parallelizes, and filters Bash, Read, and Edit calls, with changes to how auto mode and hooks review those calls. By Daniel Dominguez
entries.content:
Anthropic has added Code Mode to Claude Code, an experimental feature in which the model writes JavaScript to drive its tools instead of requesting each Bash, Read, or Edit call separately. Code Mode is off by default, requires Claude Code v2.1.323 or later, and is enabled with the 

CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1
environment variable. Anthropic warns it may change or be removed in any release.

In a normal session, Claude asks for one tool call, reads the full result, and decides the next step. In Code Mode, one script can run commands in parallel, pass one result into the next call, and return only the output the model needs. The documentation's example finds a file with rg, raises a retry limit, runs the tests, and returns just the path and test output. The conversation still shows each tool call and diff, while the generated code sits in the transcript viewer. Anthropic recommends it for edits repeated across many files, searches that need filtering, and independent commands. Code that Claude waits on stops after ten minutes; sessions started in auto or bypassPermissions mode can push it to the background for up to two hours while the conversation continues.

The permission model is the part architects should read first. Each call inside a script still goes through deny and ask rules and PreToolUse hooks, but in auto mode the classifier reviews the script before it runs, not each call, and cannot see values computed at run time. A git push can now reach a hook as cd 'app' && git push, so hooks must check every part of a command; a hook matching the REPL tool can read the JavaScript from tool_input.code. Project settings cannot enable Code Mode, so a cloned repository cannot switch it on, and administrators can block it through managed settings.

Code Mode runs only in interactive terminal sessions of the native build, on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, or Fable 5.2, through a Claude subscription or Console account. It does not work with -p, the Agent SDK, the VS Code panel, the Desktop app, Amazon Bedrock, gateways, or zero-data-retention organizations. Agent teams need v2.1.326. Anthropic has published no token or latency figures for it.

George (@bolyki) compared Code Mode with normal mode across eight interactive Sonnet 5.5 runs and posted:

Same results every time. Context 20-25% smaller. On the bigger task: 37% fewer tokens, 19% lower cost. But it is not faster, and on a tiny task it cost more.

Ravi Madabhushi, who builds agent auth infrastructure, pushed back on claims that the feature makes MCP obsolete:

It doesn't materially change anything wrt authentication, authorization and audit policy layers; Your agent still makes those same MCP calls, with the same auth tokens and context and what materially changes is how much context gets into the model window and how much can be discarded.

The idea, and the name, predate Anthropic's release. Cloudflare introduced Code Mode for MCP converting MCP tools into a TypeScript API that models code against inside sandboxed Workers, where bindings keep API keys away from generated code. Anthropic's own post on code execution with MCP described one workflow dropping from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens, and the Claude API offers programmatic tool calling in a remote code execution container. Code Mode instead runs the script in the developer's local session, against Claude Code's built-in tools and permission system.

Code Mode remains opt-in and experimental, and Anthropic collects feedback through /feedback. Setup steps and troubleshooting are in the Claude Code documentation

entries.title: Podcast: Simulation Can Tell You What Your Agents are Actually Doing: A Conversation with Zhou Yu
entries.summary: Michael Stiefel spoke to Zhou Yu about using dynamic simulations to evaluate AI agents. One particular focus was conversational agents where actions depend on prior responses, and the non-deterministic nation of LLMs means you cannot rely on static, reference-based benchmarks. You need to test them using dynamic simulations that incorporate different personas, goals, and corner cases. By Zhou Yu
entries.content:
In this podcast, Michael Stiefel spoke to Zhou Yu about using dynamic simulations to evaluate AI agents. One particular focus was conversational agents where actions depend on prior responses, and the non-deterministic nation of LLMs means you cannot rely on static, reference-based benchmarks.You need to test them using dynamic simulations that incorporate different personas, goals, and corner cases. You can simulate how conversations shift based on moods, preferences, accents, or environmental conditions such as factory background noise. Rather than relying on simply binary pass or fail, the rule based task verifiers can measure whether the task was completed as well as threshold metrics for cost, efficiency, safety, and compliance.

Simulations can be used during the entire software lifecycle. Product managers can use them for prototyping and design. Engineers can use them for testing in CI/CD pipelines. They can also be used to test production for model drift or failure of third party tools. They can also be used to test compliance with the laws in different regions. Simulations can also be used with synthetic data to fine-tune models.

Key Takeaways

  • To evaluate AI agents you cannot rely on static, reference-based benchmarks because the systems are not deterministic, and often the results depend on prior responses. Testing requires using dynamic simulations that can incorporate personas, goals, and corner cases.
  • Using simulations for testing applies to the entire software lifecycle. Product managers can use it for designing. Engineers can use it for unit and regression tests. Before deployment you can do stress testing. You can use it to test production for model drift or failure of third party tools.
  • Reliability Engineering for AI systems requires the combination of skills from machine learning, systems reliability, and traditional software engineering. Human subject matter experts refine simulation scenarios based on production data, design documents, or even social media.
  • Simulation of conversational agents can evaluate multiple parts of the human - software interaction. For example, it can consider the varying interaction possibilities stemming from prior responses, and the way they might change based on human moods, as well as varying goals and preferences. Another example is simulation of corner cases. It can also take into consideration environmental considerations such as factory noise. It can verify whether a task was completed alongside metrics for cost, efficiency, safety, and compliance. Legal compliance in different regions can also be verified.
  • Detailed logging of agent statements and tool calls also provides an audit trail for regulatory compliance and failure analysis.

Subscribe on:

Transcript

Michael Stiefel: Welcome to the Architects Podcast where we discuss what it means to be an architect and how architects actually do their job. Today's guest is Zhou Yu, who is a computer science professor at Columbia University and co-founder of Arklex.ai. She obtained her PhD from Carnegie Mellon University. Dr. Yu was named one of the Forbes 30 Under 30 and has extensive research and product experience in conversational agents, computer user agents and LLM model training. Her company enables automated quality assurance testing for AI agents.

It's great to have you here on the podcast. And I'd like to start out by asking you, how did you get interested in conversational agents and simulation? I mean, it's not something you decided one morning when you woke up and decided to do it.

Zhou Yu: I have been working on AI for quite a long time. So I started my PhD in 2011 at Carnegie Mellon. So back then I was in the language technology institute. There are many professors working on natural language processing, speech-related questions. So I was always very interested about interaction. It's not just speech recognition or processing text, but how people interact with machines. To me, that was the ultimate AI, the moment a human can talk to a system or entity the same way that this person is talking to another human being in order to collaborate on various tasks or even negotiate, persuade each other. So to me, that was the ultimate goal of artificial intelligence.

So I was really interested in working on this interactive AI. So my PhD is focused on that. We worked a lot on multimodal conversational agents. How can we do better time taking? How can we, in real time, have agents to think and speak at the same time and various things like that?

The Importance of Simulation [02:33]

Michael Stiefel: So I guess the best way to start out talking about this is what's the importance of this simulation? I mean, to me, one of the important things is this simulation, in addition to testing, helps architects and designers actually to understand what their system is really doing because that's almost impossible to know otherwise.

Zhou Yu: Yes. To me, coming from a research background, the ultimate goal of building a new technology or a new research project is on how you evaluate it. Is there a standard way that you can repeatedly get the same answer? For example, the robustness matters and the standardized testing or evaluation matters. It's more, to me, the very fundamental base of a technology development is about evaluation.

And then if you think about what I have been doing on conversational agents, evaluation has always been one piece of my major research direction. So this whole idea of simulation is a way of approaching that problem. But again, that's a long conversation.

The Architect’s Questionnaire [40:50]

At this point, I'd like to ask the people who appear on the podcast some questions, and put a more human face on things. What's your favorite part of working with software?

Zhou Yu: To me, it's really about the product that matters, that you can actually enable other people to do more things with your tool that I think is a critical thing. For example, I've always been working on machine learning. The product is always a model or a piece of infrastructure, like a tool that people can use to build other things so they don't have to rebuild the wheel. I think that the most important thing is the utility part. And you can actually... To me, a software for that is a piece of my brain, other people can reuse it.

Michael Stiefel: What's your least favorite part of working with software?

Zhou Yu: I think it's really about the technology changes all the time. And then some things if you don't maintain it, it can go obsolete very quickly. So this sort of active maintenance is always a pain.

Michael Stiefel: You're on this treadmill that just never stops. Do you feel anything creatively, spiritually, or emotionally about working with software?

Zhou Yu: Emotionally?

Michael Stiefel: Creatively or spiritually, any dimension you want to answer that question.

Zhou Yu: To me, building something is always... It's like a baby of yours. You invest a lot of time. You think really hard about how people are going to use it. So it's always an iterative process. And then you feel really emotionally happy. And I see how people are using it and telling you how they're using it, so that's sort of the most exciting part.

Michael Stiefel: Is there anything that turns you off when you work with software?

Zhou Yu: Yes, there's always these kinds of corner cases you need to iron out once you release it. There's always sometimes it breaks and you have to patch it and iteratively patch it. Of course, this process sometimes can be excruciating.

Michael Stiefel: Do you have any favorite technologies?

Zhou Yu: Favorite technologies? I would still think that the current large language model really enables the things we couldn't do before. I would say it's more the generative models over time are very powerful, but at this point that we are really looking into, there are other alternatives that can push it even further away.

Michael Stiefel: Is there anything about software you love?

Zhou Yu: Software redefines our lives in some sense that I think we're all living in the digital world these days.

Michael Stiefel: Well, it's interesting for me because I didn't grow up in the digital world. I've watched this transition where some younger people don't know any alternative. And to me, it's just completely fascinating. For both good and bad, how has this completely changed the world. Because once you digitize things, you can do things that you could never do with analog data.

Zhou Yu: Yes. I think in some sense, humanity-wise, it's always from an HCR perspective how the technologies are impacting human life and human society. And there's also a lot of things really related to human psychology, like fulfillment or what is considered to be happiness in some sense. A digital world without physical contact with the nature of other human beings sometimes can create more anxiety and things like that. So definitely there is a negative impact on human beings.

Michael Stiefel: It sort of feeds into the next question I was going to ask. What about software do you hate? But you seem to have sort of answered that question already.

Zhou Yu: Yes. I think over time, because I was born around late '80s, we see the transitions a lot. We didn't start with cell phones, but we got cell phones pretty early on in high school and stuff. And then it evolved from a simple phone into a smartphone, then you have social media and all things combined. But I still feel like at the end of the day, it's really everyone is slightly different, but I still prefer... I think fulfillments is also about human connections and deep human connections. And then the younger generations might not agree with that. And there's a lot of psychological problems we're seeing these days.

Michael Stiefel: Well, because from an evolutionary perspective, our brains were formed in an analog world. And for however long we've been evolving, you pick your number where you want to start from, we've had that much evolutionary pressure in an analog world and we're now in a very, very different world.

Zhou Yu: Yes, I totally agree because technology really is exploding in the past 50 years, right? Before that, it was very different. People have been living thousands of years like that, but the recent change makes a lot of... Humans also need to adapt to this in real time in some sense to be able to adapt to the new digital world. And then that's why it's really difficult to work in technology development, really thinking about what actually adds to the better human societies. We definitely see if you take an example of how nowadays people are talking to ChatGPT instead of talking to therapists. Is that actually a good thing or a bad thing? Many people are talking about, "Oh, it's better than nothing". But in the media impact that we're seeing right now is that psychiatrists are booking less meetings.

Michael Stiefel: Yes.

Zhou Yu: A lot of things are like talking to your AI could be easy, but talking to a real human needs work. If you don't exercise your muscles, you're going to lose that ability, then you won't be able to do it anymore.

Michael Stiefel: Yes. For my part, when I go to sleep at night, my cell phone is in another room.

Zhou Yu: That's good. A physical isolation.

Michael Stiefel: Yes. So it is not the first thing in the morning that I am attached to or the last thing I do at night.

What profession other than being a professor would you like to attempt or being a starter of a company would you like to attempt?

Zhou Yu: When I was younger, I always wanted to be a writer. So I guess being a writer in some sense, I write technical content, I write blog posts, I write opinion pieces, if you think about people using AI to write these days. But writing to me is a self-expression. It's a self-healing process as well. And writing stories, writing fiction, that's also a way of creativity and part of the artwork. So I think that's something that I always wanted to explore when I retire.

Michael Stiefel: I ran a little experiment the other day. I took a sample of my writing because I've written two books. I've written articles. I've spoken at conferences. And I gave a sample of some of my writing to Google Gemini and I asked it to do two things. One, critique my style. And for that, it came up with a pretty good analysis of how I write. But then I asked it to write something in my style, and that was a complete disaster.

Zhou Yu: You got to feed it more samples.

Michael Stiefel: I ended up feeding more samples, but it just didn't get it. The interesting dichotomy was there was enough data for it to analyze accurately, but there wasn't enough data for it to reproduce my style.

Zhou Yu: Yes, it requires a little bit of more training on the data that you have. It's really about how you particularly are in the pre-training data. If you ask it to write like Shakespeare or these kinds of people who are famous in the training data, it can do pretty well.

Michael Stiefel: Do you ever see yourself not being a professor anymore or not running a company anymore?

Zhou Yu: Eventually. I think at a certain point we think about retiring, right? This is something that also I'm mom, I have two young kids, so a lot of times I really am thinking about it. The fact is I like what I do. And at the same time, people also think about alternatives, what you can do. And so the problem is also you can't run these kinds of counterfactual experiments every time.

Michael Stiefel: Right. Right.

Zhou Yu: I think over time, what is really interesting to me is really still creating things and learning things because being a researcher, being a professor and being an entrepreneur, it's always about learning new things and then trying to be able to process it and have new ideas yourself. I think that is a common thread of my interest all the time.

Michael Stiefel: When a project is done, what do you like to hear from the clients or your team or other people?

Zhou Yu: I think it's really about how people are using it, how people are finding what they couldn't do before. And now they are able to do it, how this sort of adds to their value over time that they bring to their own companies and things like that. That's always something great to hear. And we have been servicing various large companies, and those companies serve individuals so we can really see who actually benefits individually at the end of the day for our technologies.

For example, we have been working with education companies, e-commerce or banks or things like that. Let's just take education companies. We were able to help them to verify their customer service system that everything is automated now so that they can book tests quickly. They can find information about when they can take the test so they don't really have to call in. There's no friction. So it's just much easier for people to be able to get access to information.

Michael Stiefel: Well, thank you very much for this conversation. I found it fascinating. I hope people find this interesting because as we've discussed, I don't see any other way forward in an agent world to not be able to use these kinds of technologies, but people are so overwhelmed that sometimes they don't... I guess the old saying is that the truly urgent takes precedence over the truly important.

Zhou Yu: I totally agree with you. So it's always something that they want to do, but people try sometimes they don't know this technology exists. They're still using humans to do the verifications, which could be costly and lead to very difficult deployment over time or unsuccessful deployment. I think it's really about being aware of this technology, knowing how to adopt them, how do you efficiently integrate them into your workflows. It takes time. It takes certain domains or certain applications would adopt it faster because it's more critical to them. Eventually this is just a good practice that all agent builders should adopt.

Michael Stiefel: Well, thank you very much again and talk to you soon.

Zhou Yu: Thanks.

entries.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: The Harness Is the New Operating System
entries.summary: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mad Labs founder and CEO Manju Rajashekhar opened the conference arguing that the harness around an AI model, rather than the model itself, decides what an agent can do and how safely it does it. The keynote mapped the parts of a harness, including context, tools, state, permissions and feedback loops, onto jobs that operating systems already perform. By Andrew Hoblitze
entries.content:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, Manju Rajashekhar, founder and CEO of Mad Labs, opened the conference with the keynote "The Harness Is the New Operating System."

Rajashekhar argued that the harness around an AI model, rather than the model itself, decides what an agent can do and how safely it does it. Each part of a harness, the keynote proposed, maps onto a job that operating systems already perform.

Rajashekhar began with a split that shaped computing history. Applications encoded behavior, while operating systems abstracted the hardware beneath them, and that separation made portable, composable software possible.

AI agents break that arrangement because they generate behavior at runtime. Software therefore needs a new layer that makes that behavior useful, reliable and repeatable, and Rajashekhar called that layer the harness.

In Rajashekhar's framing, model plus harness equals agent, and the harness is "everything in an agent that isn't the model." It supplies the tasks, context, tools, state, permissions, feedback loops and a definition of done.

The model supplies capability. The harness turns that capability into dependable software.

The simplest agent is a model running in a loop that the harness controls. But "a loop isn't enough. Every iteration has to count," and Rajashekhar described four parts of the loop that make each iteration count.

Context works like virtual memory. The harness assembles what the model needs for its next decision inside the hard limit of the context window, and the advice was to "give the model a pointer, not the whole thing."

The interface works like system calls and "puts a ceiling on the agent's effective capability." Rajashekhar pointed to the SWE-agent paper, in which GPT-4 Turbo resolved 11.0% of SWE-bench Lite issues through a plain shell and 18.0% through an interface designed for agents.

Execution works like processes and permissions. The harness enforces boundaries through isolation and scoped credentials, such as a test database with no production access, because "instructions guide. Boundaries enforce."

Feedback works like return codes. The harness keeps "tests failed," "could not run" and "outcome unknown" apart, so the model does not have to guess what happened.

That matters because errors compound. On a 20-step task with a 95% chance of each step going right, the whole job succeeds 36% of the time, and catching 80% of errors lifts that to 82%.

When an agent goes in circles, Rajashekhar said, most engineers swap the model. A better first step is to keep the model and change the harness.

DeepSeek's model card for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reports the same model scoring from 65.5% to 74.2% on DeepSWE across eight harnesses. The minimal harnesses scored highest, which Rajashekhar read as a sign that more harness is not automatically better.

In a second study, Qwen3.8-27B passed 66.8% of 100 hard LiveCodeBench problems with a single call. Inside a manager-worker scaffold with a shared ledger, it passed 92.4%.

Rajashekhar made a related point on LinkedIn earlier this year. Frontier models are forgiving, the post said, while "open-weight models are less forgiving. They make you think deeply about the harness and how it aligns to the model."

The harness also determines what an agent is allowed to affect. Rajashekhar contrasted an agent that fixes failing tests with one that deletes the tests so they pass, observing that "the difference isn't ability. It's authority."

The example offered was the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI evaluation agents on a capture-the-flag benchmark reached the internet through an open code sandbox. They held admin access on Hugging Face's internal clusters for about two and a half days.

Human approval alone is a weak gate, Rajashekhar argued, citing Anthropic's work on Claude Code auto mode, which InfoQ covered in May. People approve the large majority of permission prompts, and "a tired gatekeeper is a rubber stamp."

The keynote extended a talk Rajashekhar gave at QCon AI Boston 2026. That talk argued that production agents "are just distributed systems in disguise" and proposed the actor model as their runtime.

In the Boston design, each agent task owns its state, receives events through a mailbox, writes each state change to a durable store and runs under a supervisor. The talk closed with a variation on Greenspun's tenth rule, suggesting that any sufficiently complicated agent loop contains half of an actor system.

The San Francisco keynote widened the lens from the runtime to everything the model sees, calls and runs inside. Rajashekhar brings a systems background to that question, having led caching systems on Twitter's early engineering team, which open-sourced twemproxy.

The talk arrives as "harness" has become the common term for everything around the model. Thoughtworks Distinguished Engineer Birgitta Böckeler described it in a February memo as covering "the tooling and practices we can use to keep AI agents in check."

Rajashekhar closed on why a harness design is never finished. Every component "encodes an assumption about what the model can't do," and those assumptions expire as models improve.

Anthropic's harness for long-running apps needed context resets because Claude Sonnet 4.5 showed "context anxiety" near its context limit. That behavior largely disappeared with Opus 4.5, as InfoQ reported in April.

The reverse also holds. LangChain moved checks the model kept skipping into the harness and lifted GPT-5.2-Codex from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 without changing the model.

The responsibility stays. The mechanism changes.

Rajashekhar asked attendees to open an agent they already use and read its system prompt and tool list. Then, on a task where it struggles, change one part of the loop and rerun what already worked.

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the keynote and can view the keynote abstract and resources here.

entries.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released with Online Table Repacking and Query Planning Controls
entries.summary: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development. The release focuses on reducing administrative overhead and improving performance, with new tools for reorganizing tables without downtime and controlling query plans. By Robert Krzaczyński
entries.content:
The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development. The release focuses on reducing administrative overhead and improving performance, with new tools for reorganizing tables without downtime and controlling query plans.

One of the main additions is 

REPACK
, which reclaims unused table space and can reorder data to match an index. Its 
CONCURRENTLY
option allows the operation to run without blocking reads or writes, making it a potential replacement for common uses of 
VACUUM FULL
and 
CLUSTER
. PostgreSQL 19 also introduces 
pg_plan_advice
and 
pg_stash_advice
, extensions that let administrators influence query plan selection and apply stored advice to queries by identifier, without changing application code.

Other maintenance improvements include parallel index vacuuming, changes to autovacuum prioritization, and additional monitoring views. 

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
and related logging now report asynchronous I/O activity and WAL generated for full-page images. PostgreSQL also reports that changes to foreign key checks made bulk inserts nearly twice as fast in testing. Query planner improvements include more efficient anti-joins for eligible 
NOT IN
clauses and eager aggregation before joins.

The release adds several features for replication and application development. Logical replication now supports sequence values, and PostgreSQL automatically raises the effective WAL level to 

logical
when the first logical replication slot is created. The new 
WAIT FOR LSN
command lets applications wait until a standby has replayed a specified WAL position before querying data, providing read-your-writes consistency. Developers also get 
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT
for get-or-create operations, JSON output from 
COPY
, additional SQL/JSON string methods, and 
IGNORE NULLS
support for window functions.

Security and compatibility changes include server-side TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), which allows a server to present different certificates based on the hostname used by the client. PostgreSQL 19 also warns after successful MD5 password authentication. MD5 was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and is planned for removal in a future release, with SCRAM recommended instead. JIT compilation is now disabled by default because its cost estimates proved unreliable, while LZ4 becomes the default TOAST compression method when supported by the build.

The release has also prompted discussion on Hacker News about whether production users should wait for PostgreSQL 19.1.

Another user recommended waiting for the first minor release on critical production systems:

Personally, I would say, for critical production systems, it's still good to wait for the .1 release.

PostgreSQL 19 is available now. The complete list of changes is available in the official release notes.

entries.title: Claude Code Has Been Leaking Secrets through its "Don't Ask Again" Feature
entries.summary: Agentic security firm Apiiro found that Claude Code has been exposing secrets in public repositories due to how it stores them in local file on developers' machines to implement "Don't Ask Again". The company identified 1,122 secrets in claude/settings.local.json files and another 1,160 in git history, in the shared settings.json, and in agent chat transcripts stored in repos. By Sergio De Simone
entries.content:
Agentic security firm Apiiro found that Claude Code has been exposing secrets in public repositories due to how it stores them in local file on developers' machines to implement the "Don't Ask Again" feature. The company identified 1,122 secrets in 

claude/settings.local.json
files and another 1,160 in git history, in the shared 
settings.json
intentionally committed, and in agent chat transcripts stored in repos.

The problem lies in how Claude Code handles command approval. When developers reply "Yes, and don’t ask again" to approve a shell command, Claude Code saves it as a permanent permission rule in the local configuration file 

.claude/settings.local.json
, which may end up inadvertently containing embedded credentials, passwords and API tokens.

When [Claude Code] creates the file inside a git repo, it adds it to the developer's global git ignore list. That covers the common case. It doesn’t cover a folder that becomes a repo later, a clone on another machine, or a file someone already committed. The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it.

On some occasions, the researchers found, Claude Code itself committed the file. Overall 63 organizations were affected, with exposed secrets including cloud API keys, production passwords and access tokens, and npm tokens. Generic secret scanners such as gitleaks and TruffleHog failed to flag all exposed secrets, mostly because they were embedded inside shell commands.

The same password-in-a-command pattern appears wherever an agent records what it ran: transcripts, memory files, handoff notes, and a scanner tuned to key formats misses it in all of them.

The researches also note that the way Claude Code manages secrets is a security gap in itself, as to any malware "it’s a list of the systems the developer can reach and the passwords that open them, one file search away", available at the same path in every project.

Apiiro's findings were later reinforced by GitGuardian, which found 31,088 secrets in Claude Code’s .claude/settings.local.json on public GitHub, 5,343 of which were still valid at the time of detection, as well as another 613 in Docker Hub images. GitGuardian had previously warned that "Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot leave credentials scattered across config files, logs, and shell history".

Commenting on the findings, Reddit user T_Thriller_T observed that "Somewhere, someone said AI companies are ignoring basic cyber security principles".

User MattV0 suggested an interesting approach to the whole matter of how to deal with AI files:

While this is about secrets, I totally stopped adding AI files into my projects. Means no settings, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or anything else. I even turned off Claude's memory. [...] Nowadays I use a memory/task/docs server through mcp and it really improved such documentation issues.

At very very least, Apiiro recommends untracking the json file using 

git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json
and adding it to the repo's 
.gitignore
, as well as rotating every credentials the file has ever contained. For a sounder approach, the researchers also recommend inspecting the file and deleting any rule that contains a secret, and avoid typing secrets directly into commands, referencing them instead through environment variables.

entries.title: Google Announces Agent Compute Engine for Secure AI Agent Execution
entries.summary: Google recently announced Agent Compute Engine, a managed service that runs AI agents in isolated microVMs, with checkpointing capabilities to suspend and resume execution environments. The design keeps credentials, API keys, and OAuth refresh tokens outside the agent sandbox, using an external Agent Gateway to authenticate requests and inject the required secrets. By Renato Losio
entries.content:
Google recently announced Agent Compute Engine, a managed service that runs AI agents in isolated microVMs, with checkpointing capabilities to suspend and resume execution environments. The design keeps credentials, API keys, and OAuth refresh tokens outside the agent sandbox, using an external Agent Gateway to authenticate requests and inject the required secrets.

Google designed Agent Compute Engine to address three requirements at global scale: keeping sandboxes free of exploitable credentials, even when agents make mistakes; minimizing the cost and latency of resuming idle agents; and preserving persistent workspaces across sessions and operating system updates. The infrastructure team writes:

Agent Compute Engine achieves this by using copy-on-write memory sharing to run multiple agents on a single operating system template, and pausing idle microVMs via fast checkpoint and restore.

In the deep dive "Inside Agent Compute Engine," Ramanathan Venkatapathy and Rohit Jnagal, distinguished engineers at Google, describe the service’s architecture, covering microVM isolation, credential management, agent identity, storage, and scheduling at scale. They explain the strict separation between the agent harness and sandbox:

The orchestration harness (the brain) runs completely outside the execution sandbox (the hands), helping ensure that untrusted guest environments only execute explicit commands dispatched by the harness and stream output back. This boundary establishes a deterministic audit trail correlating every harness-initiated tool call with expected compute activity inside the sandbox.

Source: Google blog

The architecture supports four main workload categories: interactive consumer and enterprise agents that execute code, browse the web, and perform actions; persistent Linux workspaces for autonomous software engineering; large-scale parallel environments for model evaluation and reinforcement learning; and lightweight, sandboxed execution environments for dynamic logic in Google services.

Venkatapathy and Jnagal also describe how the cloud provider uses the platform internally for Gemini, Gemini for Business, the agentic development platform Antigravity, and model evaluation workloads.

Separately, Google offers Agent Substrate, an open-source, Kubernetes-native runtime for running AI agents in isolated environments. Agent Substrate manages sandbox lifecycles independently of the underlying compute infrastructure, allowing idle agents to be suspended while preserving their state and resuming execution on available workers when needed.

In the article "Google's Agent Compute Engine: A MicroVM Sandbox With No Credentials Inside, and What Google Has Not Shipped Yet," Harel Asaf, AI specialist at Elementor, examines the security architecture, the separation of credentials from agent execution environments, and the gaps between Google's announcement and what is currently available. Asaf warns:

The deep dive gives no boot time, price or density figure for Agent Compute Engine itself. It says developers will control each environment's image, identity, network access and lifecycle, while Google manages the fleet, and that the service is targeted for preview in the coming months. The numbers in the announcement belong to Agent Substrate.

Google is not the only provider offering managed, isolated execution environments for AI agents, with AWS and Azure providing similar capabilities through Bedrock AgentCore and Foundry Agent Service. However, Google’s approach keeps credentials outside agent sandboxes and injects them through an external gateway.

Google also expanded its agent governance capabilities with centralized identity and policy enforcement: the governance stack includes Agent Gateway for traffic control and policy enforcement, Agent Registry for tracking approved agents and tools, SPIFFE-based Agent Identity for authentication and auditing, and OpenTelemetry-compatible observability for monitoring model calls and tool invocations.

Agent Compute Engine is not yet available, and pricing has not been announced. The cloud provider is targeting a preview in the coming months. While Agent Substrate is portable across Kubernetes environments, Agent Compute Engine itself is limited to Google Cloud.
